claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge that allows selective mapping.

claims.claim: Optical stimulation of Uva axons resulted in glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three classes of retrogradely identified HVC-PNs.
claims.source: In acute brain slices we observed glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three classes of retrogradely identified HVC-PNs (27/66 HVCX, 43/51 HVCRA, 14/28 HVCAv neurons; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Optical stimulation of Uva axons resulted in significantly lower probability of observing oEPSCs in HVCX and HVCAv than in HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: Optical stimulation of Uva axons resulted in significantly lower probability of observing oEPSCs in HVCX and HVCAv than in HVCRA neurons (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Uva axon stimulation elicited relatively delayed GABAergic currents consistent with disynaptic inhibition.
claims.source: When we held the membrane voltage to +10 mV, we also observed relatively delayed GABAergic currents (53.93% probability, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with disynaptic inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the timing and pharmacological properties of the currents.

claims.claim: Uva axon stimulation elicited oIPSCs mainly in cells where oEPSCs were also observed.
claims.source: Uva axon stimulation elicited oIPSCs mainly in cells where we observed oEPSCs (oIPSC contingent with oEPSC: HVCX, 100.0%, HVCRA 96.6%, HVCAv, 95.8%; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Despite the markedly higher probability of eliciting currents in HVCRA neurons, oEPSC and oIPSC amplitudes were comparable across all the HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: Despite the markedly higher probability of eliciting currents in HVCRA neurons, oEPSC and oIPSC amplitudes were comparable across all the HVC-PN classes (Figure 2C, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: Uva terminal stimulation generally led to higher amplitude oIPSCs than oEPSCs.
claims.source: The excitation/inhibition ratio revealed that Uva terminal stimulation generally led to higher amplitude oIPSCs than oEPSCs (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Uva has been proposed to provide high-frequency (30–60 Hz) synchronous synaptic inputs that facilitate activity propagation across HVCRA premotor neurons.
claims.source: Uva has been proposed to provide high-frequency (30–60 Hz) synchronous synaptic inputs that facilitate activity propagation across HVCRA premotor neurons (Hamaguchi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Uva has been proposed to selectively drive activity in only a fraction, ~16%, of HVCRA neurons which are active during syllable transitions.
claims.source: In another proposal, Uva selectively drives activity in only a fraction,~16%, of HVCRA neurons which are active during syllable transitions (Moll et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: oEPSC returned after application of TTX + 4AP in all HVCRA neurons tested.
claims.source: Consistent with the higher likelihood of polysynaptic excitation in HVCRA neurons, we found that oEPSC returned after application of TTX +4 AP in all HVCRA neurons tested (HVCRA: 6/6 neurons) while HVCX and HVCAv were infrequently found to receive monosynaptic input from Uva (HVCX: 1/5 cells, HVCAv: 2/5 cells, Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: HVCX and HVCAv were infrequently found to receive monosynaptic input from Uva.
claims.source: Consistent with the higher likelihood of polysynaptic excitation in HVCRA neurons, we found that oEPSC returned after application of TTX +4 AP in all HVCRA neurons tested (HVCRA: 6/6 neurons) while HVCX and HVCAv were infrequently found to receive monosynaptic input from Uva (HVCX: 1/5 cells, HVCAv: 2/5 cells, Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The synaptic circuit mapping provides the first conclusive evidence that Uva makes monosynaptic connections with HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: Our synaptic circuit mapping provides the first conclusive evidence that Uva makes monosynaptic connections with HVCRA neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on the TTX+4AP experiments demonstrating monosynaptic connectivity.

claims.claim: Uva is unlikely to make monosynaptic connections with only a small percentage of HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: Given that we observed oEPSCs in 84.3% of recorded HVCRA and found monosynaptic connections from Uva onto 100% of the HVCRA neurons tested, our data further suggests that Uva is unlikely to make monosynaptic connections with only a small percentage of HVCRA neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the high probability of finding both polysynaptic and monosynaptic connections.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic oIPSCs were not observed in any cell class from Uva stimulation.
claims.source: We did not observe monosynaptic oIPSCs in any cell class, suggesting that Uva provides only a glutamatergic input to HVC (HVCX: 0/3, HVCRA: 0/5, HVCAv: 0/4, data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on the TTX+4AP experiments for inhibitory currents.

claims.claim: Uva provides only a glutamatergic input to HVC.
claims.source: We did not observe monosynaptic oIPSCs in any cell class, suggesting that Uva provides only a glutamatergic input to HVC (HVCX: 0/3, HVCRA: 0/5, HVCAv: 0/4, data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on the lack of monosynaptic inhibitory currents and in situ hybridization data.

claims.claim: Uva neurons projecting to HVC (UvaHVC) selectively expressed the glutamatergic marker SLC17A6, but not the GABAergic marker GAD1.
claims.source: We combined retrograde labeling from HVC with in-situ hybridization labeling on brain slices. This revealed that Uva neurons projecting to HVC (UvaHVC) selectively expressed the glutamatergic marker SLC17A6, but not the GABAergic marker GAD1 (Colquitt et al., 2021; Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In situ labeling did not identify any GABAergic neurons within Uva.
claims.source: Interestingly, our labeling did not identify any GABAergic neurons within Uva, indicating that UvaHVC may function as an excitatory relay of diverse polysensory input pathways.
claims.evidence: This is based on the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: UvaHVC may function as an excitatory relay of diverse polysensory input pathways.
claims.source: Interestingly, our labeling did not identify any GABAergic neurons within Uva, indicating that UvaHVC may function as an excitatory relay of diverse polysensory input pathways.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of GABAergic neurons and the known inputs to Uva.

claims.claim: NIf is a higher order polysensory DVR nucleus located adjacent to the primary auditory DVR.
claims.source: NIf is a higher order polysensory DVR nucleus located adjacent to the primary auditory DVR (Field L2 - region that receives thalamic input from the avian homologue of the medial geniculate nucleus).
claims.evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about NIf.

claims.claim: NIf is the recipient of afferents from Uva and multiple areas of the auditory DVR and has an essential role in relaying auditory signals to HVC.
claims.source: NIf is the recipient of afferents from Uva and multiple areas of the auditory DVR and has an essential role in relaying auditory signals to HVC (Coleman and Mooney, 2004).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The synaptic connection between NIf and HVC is obligatory in a young male zebra finch's ability to form a memory of their father's song.
claims.source: The synaptic connection between NIf and HVC is obligatory in a young male zebra finch's ability to form a memory of their father's song (Zhao et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Optogenetic manipulations of NIf inputs to HVC are sufficient to implant song memories that guide song syllable imitation.
claims.source: Optogenetic manipulations of NIf inputs to HVC are also sufficient to implant song memories that guide song syllable imitation (Zhao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: NIf is selectively active during singing.
claims.source: Although NIf is selectively active during singing, it is not necessary for producing song in adulthood or the song imitation process once the memory of a father's song is acquired in juvenile birds (Zhao et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2012; Mackevicius et al., 2020; Otchy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: NIf is not necessary for producing song in adulthood or the song imitation process once the memory of a father's song is acquired in juvenile birds.
claims.source: Although NIf is selectively active during singing, it is not necessary for producing song in adulthood or the song imitation process once the memory of a father's song is acquired in juvenile birds (Zhao et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2012; Mackevicius et al., 2020; Otchy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Area Avalanche is the only other nearby brain region that also sends projections to HVC.
claims.source: Area Avalanche is the only other nearby brain region that also sends projections to HVC, and we carefully checked for a lack of expression in this region in all brain hemispheres used in this study (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and verification of viral expression patterns.

claims.claim: Light stimulation reliably elicited glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three classes of HVC projection neurons from NIf.
claims.source: Light stimulation (1ms) reliably elicited glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three classes of HVC projection neurons (78.6% probability, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Optical stimulation of NIf axons resulted in strong GABAergic currents in all three classes of projection neurons.
claims.source: We examined oIPSCs in a subset of neurons and found strong GABAergic currents evoked by optical stimulation in all three classes of projection neurons (65.9% probability, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: oIPSCs from NIf stimulation were predominantly found in cells in which oEPSCs were also observed.
claims.source: oIPSCs were predominantly found in cells in which we also observed oEPSCs (oIPSC contingent with oEPSC: HVCX 90.0%; HVCRA 76.5%, HVCAv 94.1%; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: oEPSC and oIPSC amplitudes from NIf stimulation were comparable between HVCX and HVCAv PNs.
claims.source: We found oEPSC and oIPSC amplitudes to be comparable between HVCX and HVCAv PNs (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: HVCRA neurons had lower amplitude currents from NIf stimulation than the other HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: However, HVCRA neurons had lower amplitude currents than the other HVC-PN classes (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of NIf axonal terminals evoked relatively higher amplitude oIPSCs than oEPSCs in all HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: When we computed the amplitude of oEPSCs and oIPSCs for each cell to calculate the excitation/inhibition, we observed that optogenetic stimulation of NIf axonal terminals evoked relatively higher amplitude oIPSCs than oEPSCs in all HVC-PN classes (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Application of TTX followed by 4AP reliably returned oEPSCs in all three HVC projection subtypes from NIf stimulation.
claims.source: We found that application of TTX followed by 4AP reliably returned oEPSCs in all three HVC projection subtypes (monosynaptic oEPSCs: HVCX: 5/5, HVCRA: 4/5, HVCAv: 5/5, Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: NIf provides widespread monosynaptic connectivity to HVC-PNs, in stark contrast to thalamic excitatory inputs from Uva that preferentially target HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: This widespread monosynaptic connectivity is in stark contrast to thalamic excitatory inputs from Uva that preferentially target HVCRA neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on the monosynaptic connectivity data from both Uva and NIf experiments.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic oIPSCs from NIf stimulation were not observed.
claims.source: Similar to Uva projections, we did not observe monosynaptic oIPSCs (HVCX: 0/5, HVCRA: 0/2, HVCAv: 0/3, data not shown), suggestive of a glutamatergic projection from NIf to HVC.
claims.evidence: This is based on the TTX+4AP experiments for inhibitory currents.

claims.claim: NIf neurons projecting to HVC (NIfHVC) selectively expressed the glutamatergic marker SLC17A6, but not the GABAergic marker GAD1.
claims.source: We combined retrograde labeling from HVC with in situ hybridization labeling on brain slices. NIf neurons projecting to HVC (NIfHVC) selectively expressed the glutamatergic marker SLC17A6, but not the GABAergic marker GAD1 (Colquitt et al., 2021; Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: NIf projections result in disynaptic inhibition onto HVC projection neurons.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with previous studies indicating that NIf projections result in disynaptic inhibition onto HVC projection neurons (Coleman and Mooney, 2004).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature and the current data.

claims.claim: NIf provides excitatory glutamatergic monosynaptic projections onto all three known classes of HVC-PNs.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that intratelencephalic DVR circuits are excitatory and that NIf provides excitatory glutamatergic monosynaptic projections onto all three known classes of HVC-PNs.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NIf connectivity data.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic connectivity across regions of the DVR has not previously been examined.
claims.source: Given that monosynaptic connectivity across regions of the DVR has not previously been examined, this suggests the possibility that, in contrast to the thalamo-DVR pathways, projections between regions of the DVR might not have cell type selectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings and their implications.

claims.claim: Projections between regions of the DVR might not have cell type selectivity, in contrast to the thalamo-DVR pathways.
claims.source: Given that monosynaptic connectivity across regions of the DVR has not previously been examined, this suggests the possibility that, in contrast to the thalamo-DVR pathways, projections between regions of the DVR might not have cell type selectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences between Uva and NIf connectivity patterns.

claims.claim: The DVR is comprised of three large pallial fields separated by distinct lamina: the nidopallium, mesopallium, and the arcopallium.
claims.source: The DVR is comprised of three large pallial fields separated by distinct lamina: the nidopallium, mesopallium, and the arcopallium.
claims.evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about the DVR structure.

claims.claim: HVC, NIf, and mMAN reside in the nidopallium, and Av is in the mesopallium.
claims.source: HVC, NIf, and mMAN reside in the nidopallium, and Av is in the mesopallium.
claims.evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about the location of these brain regions.

claims.claim: mMAN receives synaptic input from the thalamic nucleus DMP and is part of a vocal motor DVR-thalamo-DVR loop.
claims.source: mMAN receives synaptic input from the thalamic nucleus DMP and is part of a vocal motor DVR-thalamo-DVR loop (mMAN >HVC > RA>DMP > mMAN), a circuit architecture similar to premotor and motor control-related cortico-thalamo-cortical loops in mammals.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mMAN connectivity.

claims.claim: Lesions of mMAN in juvenile zebra finches result in song imitation deficits.
claims.source: Although the synaptic connectivity between mMAN and HVC has not been well studied, lesions of mMAN in juvenile zebra finches result in song imitation deficits and lesions in adult Bengalese finches increase song syntax variability, suggesting a role in selection and planning of vocal motor sequencing (Foster and Bottjer, 2001; Koparkar et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Lesions of mMAN in adult Bengalese finches increase song syntax variability.
claims.source: Although the synaptic connectivity between mMAN and HVC has not been well studied, lesions of mMAN in juvenile zebra finches result in song imitation deficits and lesions in adult Bengalese finches increase song syntax variability, suggesting a role in selection and planning of vocal motor sequencing (Foster and Bottjer, 2001; Koparkar et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Av is reciprocally connected to HVC.
claims.source: Av is one of the more recently described song-related regions, and unlike Uva, NIf, and mMAN, it is reciprocally connected to HVC.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about Av.

claims.claim: Av is embedded in a higher order auditory portion of the DVR and thought to be an important node in the circuit comparing efferent copies of motor commands from HVC to auditory feedback.
claims.source: The role of Av is still poorly explored, but it is understood to be embedded in a higher order auditory portion of the DVR and thought to be an important node in the circuit comparing efferent copies of motor commands from HVC to auditory feedback (Bauer et al., 2008; Akutagawa and Konishi, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: mMAN provides a strong projection to Av.
claims.source: While evaluating connectivity between HVC, mMAN, and Av, we discovered that mMAN also provides a strong projection to Av (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a novel finding supported by the tracing data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Approximately half of the identified projection neurons in mMAN project to Av.
claims.source: Approximately half of the identified projection neurons in mMAN project to Av, and our tracing experiments reveal that there are only partially overlapping classes of projection neurons in mMAN: mMANHVC PNs, mMANAv PNs, and mMANHVC/AV PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There are only partially overlapping classes of projection neurons in mMAN: mMANHVC PNs, mMANAv PNs, and mMANHVC/AV PNs.
claims.source: Approximately half of the identified projection neurons in mMAN project to Av, and our tracing experiments reveal that there are only partially overlapping classes of projection neurons in mMAN: mMANHVC PNs, mMANAv PNs, and mMANHVC/AV PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The newly identified mMAN to Av pathway appears positioned to provide the auditory system with information about song motor commands via a DVR-thalamo-DVR loop.
claims.source: This newly identified pathway appears positioned to provide the auditory system with information about song motor commands via a DVR-thalamo-DVR loop (RA >DMP > mMAN>Av).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known connectivity of these regions and the newly discovered pathway.

claims.claim: The mMAN to Av pathway opens the potential for synaptic loops relaying through HVC between these regions.
claims.source: It also opens the potential for synaptic loops relaying through HVC between these regions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the newly discovered pathway and known connectivity.

claims.claim: Brain regions nearby mMAN do not send projections to HVC.
claims.source: Brain regions nearby mMAN do not send projections to HVC, and we were able to achieve robust expression of eGtACR1 in mMAN (Figure 5A), allowing us to selectively examine the synaptic connectivity between mMAN and HVC-PNs.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge and verification of viral expression patterns.

claims.claim: Optical stimulation of mMAN axon terminals revealed glutamatergic oEPSCs in all retrogradely identified projection neuron classes.
claims.source: Optical stimulation of mMAN axon terminals in brain slices revealed glutamatergic oEPSCs in all retrogradely identified projection neuron classes, albeit with significantly lower success rate compared to what we observed when stimulating NIf terminals (48.15% probability; mMAN vs. NIf oEPSC probability: Fisher's exact test p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: oEPSCs from mMAN stimulation were more likely evoked in recordings from HVCX and HVCAv than from HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: In addition, we found that oEPSCs were more likely evoked in recordings from HVCX and HVCAv than from HVCRA neurons (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mMAN axon terminals revealed GABAergic currents in all three HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: Optogenetic stimulation of mMAN axon terminals also revealed GABAergic currents in all three HVC-PN classes (48.24% probability).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: oIPSCs elicited by mMAN axons were most often found in cells where oEPSCs were also observed.
claims.source: Similar to NIf and Uva inputs, oIPSCs elicited by mMAN axons were most often found in cells where oEPSCs were also observed (oIPSC contingent with oEPSC: HVCX: 93.5%, HVCRA: 96.4%, HVCAv: 90.9%; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: oEPSCs amplitudes from mMAN stimulation across HVC-PN classes were statistically indistinguishable.
claims.source: While oEPSCs amplitudes across HVC-PN classes were statistically indistinguishable (Figure 5C), we found that oIPSCs in HVCAv had significantly higher amplitude than those evoked in HVCRA neurons (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: oIPSCs in HVCAv from mMAN stimulation had significantly higher amplitude than those evoked in HVCRA neurons.
claims.source: While oEPSCs amplitudes across HVC-PN classes were statistically indistinguishable (Figure 5C), we found that oIPSCs in HVCAv had significantly higher amplitude than those evoked in HVCRA neurons (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: GABAergic currents from mMAN stimulation had higher amplitude than glutamatergic currents.
claims.source: Despite this difference, when computing the E/I ratio, we did not see any significant difference across HVC-PNs, and like the other inputs examined, GABAergic currents had higher amplitude than glutamatergic currents (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: mMAN monosynaptically contacts all three classes of HVC PNs.
claims.source: We found evidence that mMAN monosynaptically contacts all three classes of HVC PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The most reliable monosynaptic transmission from mMAN is to HVCAv neurons and HVCX neurons.
claims.source: The most reliable monosynaptic transmission is between mMAN and HVCAv neurons and HVCX neurons (HVCRA: 2/5, HVCX: 5/7, HVCAv: 6/6, Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic oIPSCs from mMAN stimulation were not observed.
claims.source: We did not observe monosynaptic oIPSCs (HVCX: 0/5, HVCRA, 0/5, HVCAv: 0/6, data not shown), and confirmed that mMAN neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic using in-situ hybridization combined with retrograde tracing from injection of tracer in HVC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the TTX+4AP experiments for inhibitory currents.

claims.claim: mMAN neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic.
claims.source: We did not observe monosynaptic oIPSCs (HVCX: 0/5, HVCRA, 0/5, HVCAv: 0/6, data not shown), and confirmed that mMAN neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic using in-situ hybridization combined with retrograde tracing from injection of tracer in HVC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: mMAN predominantly provides robust monosynaptic excitatory input to HVCAv and HVCX neurons.
claims.source: Together, this data indicates that mMAN predominantly provides robust monosynaptic excitatory input to HVCAv and HVCX neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mMAN connectivity data.

claims.claim: HVCAv neurons only comprise ~3% of the neurons in HVC.
claims.source: HVCAv neurons only comprise ~3% of the neurons in HVC (Roberts et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: 100% of the HVCAv neurons tested receive monosynaptic input from mMAN, suggesting that this is likely to be a highly selective synaptic target of mMAN inputs to HVC.
claims.source: Therefore, finding that 100% of the HVCAv neurons tested receive monosynaptic input from mMAN, suggesting that this is likely to be a highly selective synaptic target of mMAN inputs to HVC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the high rate of monosynaptic connectivity and the small population size of HVCAv neurons.

claims.claim: mMAN is providing Av song-related signals directly and indirectly via projections onto HVCAv neurons.
claims.source: Given that we have now also identified a projection from mMAN directly to Av, this supports a model in which mMAN is providing Av song-related signals directly and indirectly via projections onto HVCAv neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the newly discovered mMAN to Av pathway and the strong mMAN to HVCAv connectivity.

claims.claim: Avalanche lacks clear anatomical boundaries.
claims.source: Avalanche lacks clear anatomical boundaries, and our viral expression did spread into surrounding brain regions, but only brain hemispheres in which we could verify a lack of expression in NIf were included in this study (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a technical limitation in the study.

claims.claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from identified HVC-PN classes revealed glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three cell classes from Av stimulation.
claims.source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from identified HVC-PN classes in brain slices revealed glutamatergic oEPSCs in all three cell classes, yet most of the cells were not excited by Av terminals (39.18% probability; Av vs. NIf oEPSC probability: Fisher's exact test p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The probability of evoking oEPSCs from Av stimulation was similar among HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: However, the probability of evoking oEPSCs was similar among HVC-PN classes (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: GABAergic currents from Av stimulation were found in all three projection subtypes.
claims.source: We tested the presence of oIPSCs in a subset of cells and found GABAergic currents in all three projection subtypes (43.24% probability, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: oIPSCs from Av stimulation were mainly observed in HVC-PNs also showing oEPSCs.
claims.source: As in other pathways already described, we observed oIPSCs mainly in HVC-PNs also showing oEPSCs (oIPSC contingent with oEPSC: HVCX 100.0% HVCRA 90.0%, HVCAv 84.6%; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: oEPSCs amplitudes from Av stimulation were broadly similar among HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: While oEPSCs amplitudes were broadly similar among HVC-PN classes (Figure 6C), oIPSCs had significantly smaller amplitude in HVCRA compared to those evoked in HVCX neurons (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: oIPSCs from Av stimulation had significantly smaller amplitude in HVCRA compared to those evoked in HVCX neurons.
claims.source: While oEPSCs amplitudes were broadly similar among HVC-PN classes (Figure 6C), oIPSCs had significantly smaller amplitude in HVCRA compared to those evoked in HVCX neurons (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: HVCRA neurons had a significantly higher E/I ratio from Av stimulation compared to HVCX.
claims.source: Consistently, this was also reflected in a significantly higher E/I ratio in HVCRA compared to HVCX.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Av axon terminal stimulation elicited stronger GABAergic currents than glutamatergic currents across HVC-PN classes.
claims.source: Similar to the other afferents, Av axon terminal stimulation elicited stronger GABAergic currents than glutamatergic currents across HVC-PN classes (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic transmission from Av onto HVCX neurons was consistently observed.
claims.source: When examining which HVC-PN neuron classes received monosynaptic input from Av, we consistently observed monosynaptic transmission onto HVCX neurons (HVCX 4/5 cells monosynaptically contacted).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic transmission from Av onto HVCRA and HVCAv was less common.
claims.source: Monosynaptic transmission onto HVCRA and HVCAv was less common (HVCRA 2/5, HVCAv 2/6; Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the TTX+4AP experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Previous reports indicated that Av neurons projecting to HVC are excitatory.
claims.source: Previous reports indicated that Av neurons projecting to HVC are excitatory (Roberts et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Monosynaptic oIPSCs from Av stimulation were not observed across HVC-PNs.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we didn't observe any monosynaptic oIPSC across HVC-PNs (monosynaptic oIPSCs: HVCX 0/4, HVCRA 0/3, HVCAv 0/3, data not shown) and further confirmed that AvHVC neurons are glutamatergic by in situ hybridization labeling of retrogradely identified neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The study provides the first large-scale, cell-type-specific synaptic wiring diagram for sensorimotor circuits in zebra finch song learning and production. Using viral expression of eGtACR1 and whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from retrogradely labeled HVC projection neurons, the authors mapped synaptic connectivity from 4 main afferent pathways (NIf, Uva, mMAN, Av) onto three classes of HVC projection neurons (HVCX, HVCRA, HVCAv) in adult male zebra finches.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C25-C31 collectively establish the methodological approach and scope of the study. The experimental design combining optogenetics, retrograde tracing, and electrophysiology is well-documented in Figures 1-6, with hundreds of recorded neurons providing comprehensive polysynaptic and monosynaptic connectivity data across 12 afferent-HVC-PN combinations.

results.result: Uva provides predominantly monosynaptic glutamatergic input to HVCRA neurons. Optical stimulation of Uva axons elicited oEPSCs in all three HVC-PN classes, but with significantly higher probability in HVCRA neurons (84.3%) compared to HVCX (40.9%) and HVCAv (50.0%). TTX+4AP experiments confirmed monosynaptic connectivity in 100% of tested HVCRA neurons (6/6) versus infrequent monosynaptic input to HVCX (1/5) and HVCAv (2/5). In situ hybridization confirmed that Uva neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic (SLC17A6+, GAD1-).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C50 are strongly supported by converging evidence from electrophysiology (Figure 2B-F), TTX+4AP experiments demonstrating monosynaptic connectivity, and molecular confirmation via in situ hybridization (Figure 2G). The data provide the first conclusive evidence for monosynaptic Uva-HVCRA connections and contradict prior proposals that Uva contacts only ~16% of HVCRA neurons.

results.result: NIf provides widespread monosynaptic glutamatergic input to all three HVC-PN classes. Light stimulation of NIf terminals elicited oEPSCs in 78.6% of HVC-PNs across all three classes with no significant difference in probability between cell types. TTX+4AP experiments confirmed monosynaptic connectivity to all three HVC-PN subtypes (HVCX: 5/5, HVCRA: 4/5, HVCAv: 5/5). In situ hybridization confirmed NIf neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic. This contrasts with the cell-type-selective connectivity from Uva.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C69 are well-supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 3B-F), TTX+4AP experiments demonstrating widespread monosynaptic connectivity, and molecular confirmation (Figure 3G). The finding of non-selective monosynaptic connectivity from NIf to all HVC-PN classes is a novel discovery that contrasts with thalamic inputs, suggesting different connectivity rules for DVR-DVR versus thalamo-DVR pathways.

results.result: The study discovered a novel projection from mMAN to Av. Retrograde tracing revealed that approximately half of identified mMAN projection neurons project to Av, with three partially overlapping populations: mMANHVC, mMANAv, and mMANHVC/Av. This pathway is positioned to provide the auditory system with information about song motor commands via a DVR-thalamo-DVR loop (RA→DMP→mMAN→Av).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 are supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4, including both retrograde labeling and BDA anterograde labeling. This is a novel anatomical discovery that reveals previously unknown connectivity in the song circuit. The functional interpretation (C82-C83) is reasonable inference based on known circuit architecture.

results.result: mMAN provides selective monosynaptic glutamatergic input predominantly to HVCAv and HVCX neurons. Optical stimulation of mMAN terminals elicited oEPSCs in 48.15% of HVC-PNs, with higher probability in HVCX and HVCAv than HVCRA. TTX+4AP experiments revealed reliable monosynaptic transmission to HVCAv (6/6) and HVCX (5/7) but sparse connectivity to HVCRA (2/5). Given that HVCAv neurons comprise only ~3% of HVC neurons, the 100% monosynaptic connectivity rate suggests HVCAv is a highly selective target of mMAN.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C99 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 5B-E), TTX+4AP experiments (Figure 5F), and in situ hybridization confirmation of glutamatergic identity. The selective targeting of HVCAv neurons is particularly well-supported given the small population size and 100% connectivity rate. The functional interpretation linking this to the newly discovered mMAN→Av pathway is reasonable inference.

results.result: Av provides monosynaptic glutamatergic input preferentially to HVCX neurons. Optical stimulation of Av terminals elicited oEPSCs in 39.18% of HVC-PNs with similar probability across cell types. However, TTX+4AP experiments revealed consistent monosynaptic transmission to HVCX neurons (4/5) but less frequent connectivity to HVCRA (2/5) and HVCAv (2/6). In situ hybridization confirmed Av neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C114 are supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 6B-E), TTX+4AP experiments (Figure 6F), and molecular confirmation (Figure 6 supplement 1E). The authors acknowledge technical limitations with Av (C100, C196) including viral expression spreading and low expression levels, but the within-bird comparison across all three HVC-PN classes helps control for this limitation (C197).

results.result: Long-range sensory pathways to HVC show cell-type-specific biases in monosynaptic connectivity. NIf monosynaptically contacts all three HVC-PN classes, Uva predominantly contacts HVCRA neurons, mMAN preferentially contacts HVCAv and HVCX neurons, and Av predominantly contacts HVCX neurons. These connections are not stochastic but strongly biased toward specific projection pathways, revealing a modular organization with multiple intermingled loops across HVC input-output circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C134 synthesize the monosynaptic connectivity findings from all four afferents. The differential connectivity patterns are well-supported by TTX+4AP experiments across Figures 2-6. The interpretation of modular organization and intermingled loops (C134) is reasonable inference based on the observed connectivity patterns combined with the newly discovered mMAN→Av pathway.

results.result: All four afferents establish polysynaptic contact with all three HVC-PN classes, with both glutamatergic and GABAergic transmission. Across all inputs, oIPSCs were predominantly found in cells that also showed oEPSCs (90-100% contingency), suggesting compartmentalized neuronal ensembles including both projection neurons and interneurons. This organization may allow integration of afferent inputs within hyper-local networks or modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C174 are supported by the consistent observation of both oEPSCs and oIPSCs across all pathways (Figures 2-6), with high contingency between excitation and inhibition in the same cells. The interpretation of compartmentalized ensembles and modular organization is reasonable inference based on the data, though the authors acknowledge limitations in fully characterizing interneuron connectivity (C170-C172).

results.result: Analysis by HVC-PN type reveals biased afferent inputs: HVCX and HVCAv neurons are most frequently excited by NIf, while HVCRA neurons are most frequently excited by Uva and unlikely to be excited by mMAN. HVCX and HVCAv neurons are most strongly driven by NIf, while HVCRA neurons receive relatively uniform amplitude oEPSCs from all four inputs. NIf and mMAN stimulation resulted in higher amplitude inhibition onto HVCAv neurons than Uva or Av stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C158 are supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, which reorganizes the data by postsynaptic cell type. This provides a complementary view of the connectivity patterns and reveals cell-type-specific biases in both probability and amplitude of synaptic responses.

results.result: The observed polysynaptic inhibition likely involves both feedback and feedforward inhibition mechanisms. Previous studies show HVC-PNs disynaptically inhibit other HVC-PNs (feedback inhibition), and afferents may also contact neighboring interneurons (feedforward inhibition). These mechanisms are well-documented in cortical circuits and serve to control excitatory-inhibitory balance and improve network sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C169 are based on prior literature (citations provided) and reasonable inference from the observed patterns of excitation and inhibition. However, the authors acknowledge that distinguishing between feedback and feedforward mechanisms requires monosynaptic connectivity mapping of afferents onto interneurons (C170), which was not performed due to technical limitations (C171). The speculation is well-grounded but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The study has methodological limitations related to slice orientation. All recordings were performed in 230-µm-thick sagittal slices, which may have disrupted mediolateral organization of interneurons. This could account for the lack of lateral inhibition in the data, though differences between HVC and neocortical microcircuitry may also reduce the significance of lateral inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C181 represent the authors' critical self-assessment of methodological limitations. The concern about slice orientation affecting interneuron connectivity is reasonable given prior literature (C177), though the authors also note alternative explanations (C181). This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens the overall evaluation.

results.result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: (1) all recordings were from adult male zebra finches, not juveniles or females; (2) ex vivo slices may alter neuronal properties and sever some afferents; (3) optical stimulation recruits all eGtACR1-expressing fibers simultaneously; (4) viral expression efficiency varied across pathways, particularly low in Av. Future studies should examine developmental changes, employ minimal stimulation, and characterize other inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C197 represent comprehensive acknowledgment of study limitations. The authors transparently discuss scope limitations (C187-C188), technical limitations of the slice preparation (C189-C191), stimulation approach (C192-C194), and viral expression variability (C195-C197). They also describe how experimental design helps mitigate some concerns (e.g., within-bird comparisons for Av, C197).

results.result: The connectivity patterns have functional implications for song learning and production. Uva's monosynaptic connections to HVCRA may directly affect the song motor pathway and integrate with forward models of song timing. mMAN's strong connections to HVCAv and the newly discovered mMAN→Av pathway may contribute to syllable ordering. mMAN and Av's preferential connections to HVCX may create a bridge linking thalamus, auditory system, and basal ganglia circuits for song plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C150 represent functional interpretations and speculations based on the anatomical connectivity findings combined with prior functional studies. While the anatomical data are solid, the functional implications are largely speculative (note use of 'may' throughout). Some claims are supported by recent literature (C136, C140), but direct functional validation of these specific connectivity patterns was not performed in this study.

results.result: Despite distinct developmental origins, HVC projection neurons have similar gene expression and connectivity patterns to mammalian intratelencephalic neurons, suggesting evolutionary convergence. The connectivity patterns revealed in this study provide insights into synaptic underpinnings of vocal learning and production, and may offer insights into circuits for human language learning and production.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 are supported by prior literature (Colquitt et al., 2021), but the broader implications for understanding human language circuits (C201) are speculative. While the songbird-human comparison is a well-established framework in the field, the direct relevance of these specific connectivity patterns to human language remains to be demonstrated. The claim is reasonable but represents future potential rather than demonstrated findings.

results.result: The study provides a comprehensive synaptic wiring diagram for sensorimotor circuits in zebra finch song learning and production by examining functional synaptic connectivity from 4 main sensory afferent pathways (Uva, NIf, mMAN, Av) onto three classes of HVC projection neurons using viral expression of eGtACR1 combined with whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from retrogradely identified neurons. This represents the first large-scale cell-type-specific synaptic connectivity mapping using gold-standard electrophysiological methods in songbirds and the first long-range cellular resolution synaptic connectivity map in the avian DVR.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core contribution. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide compelling evidence of synaptic connections between 4 major auditory inputs...within three projection neurons in the HVC' and that they 'provided detailed map synaptic connection.' Reviewer 3 describes the study as 'remarkable in the amount of information that it generates' and states it 'makes an important contribution to increasing our identification...of the basic synaptic elements that make up the circuit organization of HVC.' The editor notes the study is 'fundamental' and provides 'compelling evidence.'

results.result: Uva (thalamic input) predominantly makes monosynaptic glutamatergic connections with HVCRA neurons (100% of tested HVCRA neurons showed monosynaptic input in TTX+4AP experiments), with significantly lower probability of monosynaptic connections to HVCX and HVCAv neurons. Uva stimulation elicited oEPSCs in 84.3% of HVCRA neurons but only 40.9% of HVCX and 50% of HVCAv neurons. All Uva neurons projecting to HVC express the glutamatergic marker SLC17A6 but not GABAergic marker GAD1, and no monosynaptic inhibitory currents were observed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'provide compelling evidence of synaptic connections' and specifically mentions 'all areas give monosynaptic excitatory inputs.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the 'careful characterization and quantification of synaptic inputs into HVC' and notes the study is 'rigorous in its implementation.' The cell-type specific connectivity pattern from Uva is presented as a key finding distinguishing thalamic from cortical inputs.

results.result: NIf (auditory DVR nucleus) provides widespread monosynaptic glutamatergic connectivity to all three HVC-PN classes with high probability (78.6% overall), in stark contrast to Uva's preferential targeting of HVCRA neurons. TTX+4AP experiments confirmed monosynaptic excitatory connections to all three cell types (HVCX: 5/5, HVCRA: 4/5, HVCAv: 5/5). NIf neurons projecting to HVC selectively expressed SLC17A6 but not GAD1, and no monosynaptic inhibitory currents were observed, though strong polysynaptic GABAergic currents were found.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as part of the comprehensive connectivity map. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provided detailed map synaptic connection' and notes 'proportions of projection to each projection neuron varied.' The editor specifically mentions the study clarifies 'how four distinct inputs to HVC act on these distinct HVC cell types' and notes they 'exhibit cell-type specific preferences in monosynaptic input strength.' The contrast between NIf's widespread connectivity and Uva's selectivity is a key finding.

results.result: mMAN (part of a vocal motor DVR-thalamo-DVR loop) provides monosynaptic glutamatergic input to all three HVC-PN classes, but most reliably to HVCAv neurons (6/6, 100%) and HVCX neurons (5/7), with sparse connections to HVCRA neurons (2/5). Given that HVCAv neurons comprise only ~3% of HVC neurons, the 100% monosynaptic connectivity rate suggests mMAN highly selectively targets this small population. mMAN neurons projecting to HVC are glutamatergic (confirmed by in situ hybridization).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without objection. Reviewer 1 notes the 'thorough and detailed analysis provide compelling evidence' and that 'proportions of projection to each projection neuron varied.' Reviewer 3 describes the work as 'rigorous in its implementation' and notes the 'tremendous labor involved for each experiment.' The selective targeting of the small HVCAv population by mMAN is presented as a significant finding about circuit organization.

results.result: Circuit tracing revealed a novel projection from mMAN to Av, with approximately half of identified mMAN projection neurons projecting to Av. There are partially overlapping classes of projection neurons in mMAN: mMANHVC PNs, mMANAv PNs, and mMANHVC/Av PNs. This newly identified pathway appears positioned to provide the auditory system with information about song motor commands via a DVR-thalamo-DVR loop (RA→DMP→mMAN→Av).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this novel finding. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'They also find specific reciprocal connections between mMAN and Av' as a strength of the study. The editor's summary mentions the study identifies 'novel connections' though does not specify which ones. Reviewer 3 notes the study makes 'an important contribution' to understanding circuit organization. No reviewer challenges this anatomical finding.

results.result: Av (reciprocally connected to HVC) provides monosynaptic excitatory input to all three HVC-PN classes, but most consistently to HVCX neurons (4/5 cells showed monosynaptic connections), with less frequent connections to HVCRA (2/5) and HVCAv (2/6). Overall probability of evoking oEPSCs was lower than other inputs (39.18%). AvHVC neurons are glutamatergic (confirmed by in situ hybridization), with no monosynaptic inhibitory currents observed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the comprehensive connectivity analysis. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'provided detailed map synaptic connection' covering all four inputs. Reviewer 3 acknowledges the 'careful characterization and quantification' of inputs. The lower viral expression in Av is acknowledged by the authors as a potential limitation, but reviewers do not challenge the relative connectivity patterns observed.

results.result: All four afferent pathways (Uva, NIf, mMAN, Av) consistently establish polysynaptic contact with all three HVC-PN classes, with both glutamatergic and GABAergic polysynaptic neurotransmission reliably observed. There is a remarkable correspondence in the probability of finding oIPSCs and oEPSCs in the same postsynaptic neurons across all inputs (oIPSC contingent with oEPSC: typically >90%), indicative of highly interconnected cell assemblies and a rich interneuronal inhibitory network recruited by afferent stimulation.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly highlights this finding, stating the authors 'provide compelling evidence that all long range projections engage inhibitory circuits in HVC.' Reviewer 1 notes 'all areas give monosynaptic excitatory inputs and polysynaptic inhibitory inputs.' Reviewer 3 describes the work as providing 'careful characterization' of inputs. The consistent pattern of co-occurring excitation and inhibition is treated as a key organizational principle of the circuit.

results.result: The connectivity patterns reveal that long-range sensory pathways to HVC are excitatory and contact HVC intratelencephalic projection neurons, but these connections are not stochastic—they are strongly biased to make synapses with specific projection pathways (premotor HVCRA, auditory HVCAv, or basal ganglia HVCX). The data indicate a modular organization of ensemble-like networks for integrating long-range input with local circuits, with multiple intermingled loops coexisting across HVC input and output circuits.
results.evaluation: The editor emphasizes that the study shows inputs 'exhibit cell-type specific preferences in monosynaptic input strength,' directly supporting the non-stochastic, biased connectivity claim. Reviewer 1 notes 'proportions of projection to each projection neuron varied,' consistent with selective targeting. Reviewer 3 states the work provides understanding of 'how external inputs...contribute to the intrinsic computations within this critic circuit.' The modular organization interpretation is accepted as a synthesis of the findings.

results.result: The study employed viral expression of eGtACR1 (blue light-driven Cl- channels that are depolarizing at axon terminals) paired with whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from visually targeted HVC projection neurons identified using retrograde tracer injections, permitting the first large-scale cell-type-specific synaptic connectivity mapping using gold-standard electrophysiological methods in songbirds.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly identifies as a strength that 'The authors optimized optogenetical tools with eGtACR1 by using AAV which allow them to manipulate synaptic inputs in a projection-specific manner in zebra finches' and that 'With their technical advance and thorough experiments, they provided detailed map.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The quality of the recordings is extremely high and the quantity of data is on a very significant scale.' Reviewer 3 describes the study as 'rigorous in its implementation.'

results.result: All circuit mapping was carried out in brain slices from adult male zebra finches, representing a limitation in scope. Future studies will be needed to examine connectivity patterns in juveniles during vocal learning phases and in female birds.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly identifies as a weakness: 'As this study is in adult brain slices, there might be a gap to the functions in developmental song learning.' The authors acknowledge this limitation in the manuscript. Reviewer 3 notes the manuscript is 'thoughtful regarding its limitations.' This is treated as a scope limitation rather than a flaw in the current findings.

results.result: The ex vivo brain slice approach has inherent limitations: intrinsic activity patterns may change in acute slices, the slicing procedure severs neuromodulatory and neurotransmitter afferents, and the axonal terminal optical manipulation recruits all fibers expressing eGtACR1 simultaneously. Additionally, viral expression efficiency varied across pathways, with notably low levels in Av potentially skewing results.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the manuscript is 'thoughtful regarding its limitations' and that 'My comments are minor and primarily about legibility, clarification of certain manipulations.' The authors explicitly acknowledge these technical limitations in the manuscript. Reviewers do not challenge the validity of the approach despite these limitations, treating them as inherent to the methodology rather than undermining the conclusions.

results.result: Distinguishing between feedback and feedforward inhibition circuit motifs will require monosynaptic connectivity mapping of afferents onto HVC interneurons, which is currently limited by the lack of genetic methods for labeling interneurons. A complete description of HVC circuitry will also require examination of other potential inputs (RAHVC PNs, NCM, A11 glutamatergic neurons) and characterization of interneuron synaptic connectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as acknowledged limitations and future directions. Reviewer 3 notes the manuscript is 'thoughtful regarding its limitations.' The authors clearly state these as gaps to be addressed in future work. Reviewers do not criticize the current study for not addressing interneuron connectivity, treating it as beyond the scope of the present work.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the core methodological approach and scope (C3, C4, C25, C27-C31) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the technical execution with hundreds of recorded neurons across 12 combinations. Peer review emphasizes the fundamental contribution and compelling evidence, with explicit praise for the optogenetic optimization. Peer review additionally includes C5, C6, C26, C115 not in OpenEval R1.

Both strongly support the Uva-HVCRA monosynaptic connectivity findings (C34-C50) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights this as first conclusive evidence contradicting prior proposals. Peer review accepts findings without challenge and notes cell-type specific connectivity as key distinguishing feature of thalamic inputs. Peer review includes C131 (differential connectivity summary) not in OpenEval R2.

Both evaluate NIf's widespread monosynaptic connectivity (C57-C69) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the novel discovery of non-selective connectivity contrasting with thalamic inputs. Peer review affirms the comprehensive connectivity map and notes the contrast between NIf's widespread connectivity and Uva's selectivity. Peer review includes C130 (summary claim) not in OpenEval R3.

Both evaluate the novel mMAN→Av anatomical pathway (C79-C83) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval focuses on the anatomical tracing evidence and reasonable functional inference. Peer review explicitly identifies this as a strength ('specific reciprocal connections between mMAN and Av') and acknowledges it as a novel finding. Peer review includes C7 not in OpenEval R4.

Both evaluate mMAN's selective targeting of HVCAv neurons (C84-C99) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the 100% connectivity rate to the small HVCAv population and links to the newly discovered mMAN→Av pathway. Peer review accepts findings as part of comprehensive analysis and notes the selective targeting as significant for circuit organization. Peer review includes C132 (summary) not in OpenEval R5.

Both evaluate Av→HVC connectivity patterns (C100-C114) as SUPPORTED despite technical limitations. OpenEval acknowledges viral expression challenges but notes within-bird comparisons help control for this. Peer review accepts findings as part of comprehensive connectivity analysis without challenging the relative patterns. Peer review includes C133 (summary) not in OpenEval R6.

Both evaluate the differential, non-stochastic connectivity patterns (C126-C134) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval synthesizes monosynaptic findings and interprets modular organization as reasonable inference. Peer review emphasizes cell-type specific preferences in input strength and accepts modular organization as synthesis. Peer review R8 includes C8 (summary claim) not in OpenEval R7.

Both evaluate the consistent co-occurrence of excitation and inhibition (C151-C152, C159-C160, C162) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes high contingency across all pathways and interprets compartmentalized ensembles while acknowledging interneuron connectivity limitations. Peer review explicitly highlights that 'all long range projections engage inhibitory circuits' as compelling evidence and treats this as a key organizational principle. Peer review R7 includes additional connectivity claims (C36-C37, C59-C60, C87-C88, C103-C104, C128-C129) showing broader scope.

OpenEval evaluates the postsynaptic cell-type reorganization analysis (C153-C158, Figure 7 supplement 1) as SUPPORTED, revealing cell-type-specific biases. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this complementary analytical perspective.

Both evaluate the limitations regarding interneuron connectivity mechanisms (C163-C172) as acknowledged gaps. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct demonstration of feedback vs feedforward mechanisms, noting speculation is well-grounded but not demonstrated. Peer review (R12) accepts these as acknowledged limitations and future directions, treating them as beyond current scope. Peer review also includes C198 (future directions).

OpenEval evaluates the authors' self-assessment of slice orientation and methodological limitations (C176-C181) as SUPPORTED, treating transparent discussion as strengthening the evaluation. No direct corresponding peer review result, though peer R11 addresses overlapping technical limitations.

Both evaluate technical and methodological limitations as SUPPORTED/acknowledged. OpenEval comprehensively lists scope, slice preparation, stimulation, and viral expression limitations (C187-C197). Peer review notes manuscript is 'thoughtful regarding its limitations' and treats them as inherent to methodology rather than undermining conclusions. Substantial overlap in claims C189-C196.

Both address scope limitations. OpenEval R12 includes adult vs developmental limitations (C187-C188) among broader limitations discussion. Peer review R10 specifically identifies as weakness the gap between adult slice findings and developmental song learning functions, which authors acknowledge. Peer R10 treats this as scope limitation rather than flaw.

OpenEval evaluates functional interpretations and speculations (C135-C150) as UNCERTAIN, noting anatomical data are solid but functional implications are largely speculative without direct validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these functional speculation claims.

OpenEval evaluates implications for human language circuits (C119-C121, C199-C201) as UNCERTAIN, noting the songbird-human comparison framework is established but direct relevance of these specific connectivity patterns remains to be demonstrated. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these translational implications.

Partial overlap on methodological approach (C25, C27-C28). OpenEval R1 evaluates overall experimental design as SUPPORTED. Peer review R9 specifically praises the technical optimization of optogenetic tools (eGtACR1 with AAV) and recording quality/quantity, identifying these as explicit strengths. Both affirm methodological rigor but peer review provides more granular technical praise.

Peer review R9 evaluates technical optimization and recording quality (C25-C28) as SUPPORTED strength, with explicit praise for optogenetic tool development and data quality/scale. While OpenEval R1 includes some overlapping claims, peer R9's specific focus on technical innovation as a distinct strength is not separately evaluated in OpenEval results.
